 Promised SPF50, Delivered SPF14: Consumer Test Exposes Sunscreen Shortfall 
 Friday, 30 October 2026, 9:11 am 
 Press Release: Consumer NZ 
 Seven out of 10 sunscreens recently tested by Consumer NZ
failed to meet their SPF label claims. While six still
offered high protection, one of the most expensive products
promised SPF50 but delivered just SPF14.
 (Photo/Supplied) Coola
Zinc Oxide Sunscreen Lotion 50 tested at just SPF14. This
product offers low protection, and is way off the factor 50
promised on its label. At $69 per 100ml, it was one of the
priciest products Consumer tested.
 “If a sunscreen
label says SPF50, New Zealanders should be able to trust
it,” says Belinda Castles, researcher at Consumer
NZ.
 “New Zealand has one of the highest skin cancer
and melanoma rates in the world. Skin cancer is largely
preventable, and we rely on sunscreens to protect us from
the sun’s harsh rays.”
 Consumer tested 10 widely
available sunscreens, priced from $4 to $76 per 100ml, to
check whether their SPF and broad-spectrum claims stacked
up.
 SPF measures protection against UVB rays, the main
cause of sunburn. Broad-spectrum sunscreens also protect
against UVA rays, which penetrate deep into the skin and can
cause wrinkles and age spots. Both UVA and UVB rays can
cause skin cancer.
 The good news: every product tested
met the requirements for broad-spectrum protection based on
the tested SPF. The bad news: only 3 out of 10 met their SPF
claims.
 Advertisement - scroll to continue reading 
 Consumer’s test found that a higher price
did not guarantee premium protection.
 “The cheapest
product we tested met its label claims. Smart365 Sun
Sunscreen Lotion SPF50+ costs $4 per 100ml,” says
Castles.
 Similarly, the Cancer Society Everyday
Protection SPF50 met its claims and costs $9 per
100ml.
 “The other six sunscreens that did not meet
label claims still offered high protection of SPF 30 or
higher – they just didn’t deliver the SPF promised on
the label,” says Castles.
 Last year, testing
undertaken by Australian advocacy organisation Choice
found similarly woeful results.
 “Choice’s test
found 16 out of 20 tested sunscreens didn’t meet their SPF
claims. Eleven of those products were sold in New Zealand
too,” says Castles.
 Sunscreen regulation
 The
Sunscreen (Product Safety Standard) Act 2022 requires
sunscreens to comply with the Australian and New Zealand
sunscreen standard, which requires independent testing.
There’s no rule on how often sunscreens must be tested.
Previous Consumer investigations have found some companies
rely on test reports that are several years
old.
 “Our latest test results show why regular
sunscreen testing is essential. Consumers should be able to
trust what’s printed on a product label,” says
Castles.
 Consumer has shared its latest findings with
the Commerce Commission.
 Shop with
confidence
 With support from Health New Zealand Te
Whatu Ora, New Zealand’s most comprehensive database of
sunscreens is hosted on Consumer
NZ’s website for all New Zealanders.
 The
sunscreen database allows users to filter products by price,
SPF, water resistance and the last time a sunscreen was
tested.
 “The database has been designed to help
people to make the best possible decision about sun
protection for themselves and their households,” says
Castles.
